scenes.visual: Title card 'Two Forests, One Bird' over two small woodland cartoons and a nest box. Same colour map as the first film: GOLD = what the species needs (here, the caterpillar food peak); GREEN = the species (here, the nestling period); RED bracket = the gap; ORANGE tint = warming. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: If a bird lays its eggs earlier every spring, is it keeping up? The first film measured a gap in space, between a species and its isotherm. This film measures a similar gap in time.
scenes.visual: A brief recap thumbnail of the first film's mountain, GOLD line above GREEN band with the RED bracket, slides away and turns sideways into a horizontal spring calendar strip (March to July).
scenes.narration: If a bird lays its eggs earlier every spring, is it keeping up? The first film measured a gap in space, between a species and its isotherm. This film measures a similar gap in time.

scenes.tts: The seasonal timing of life events is called phenology. Leafing, flowering, migration and egg laying are all phenology. As springs have warmed, many of these now come earlier.
scenes.visual: Small icons pop onto the calendar strip: a leaf, a flower, a flying bird, an egg. An ORANGE tint washes over the strip and each icon slides a little to the left, labelled 'earlier'.
scenes.narration: The seasonal timing of life events is called phenology. Leafing, flowering, migration and egg laying are all phenology. As springs have warmed, many of these now come earlier.

scenes.tts: Now one bird and its food. The gold curve is the caterpillar peak, the food supply. The green bar is when nestlings need feeding most. Here they start in step.
scenes.visual: On the calendar strip, a GOLD bell-shaped curve labelled 'caterpillar peak (food)' and a GREEN bar labelled 'nestlings in the nest (demand)' sit exactly on top of each other. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Now one bird and its food. The gold curve is the caterpillar peak, the food supply. The green bar is when nestlings need feeding most. Here they start in step.

scenes.tts: Warm the springs. The gold peak slides earlier. The green bar slides earlier too, but by less. A red bracket can open between them.
scenes.visual: ORANGE tint deepens over a years counter. The GOLD curve slides left; the GREEN bar slides left by a smaller, unlabelled amount (schematic). A RED bracket opens between the GOLD peak and the GREEN bar's centre.
scenes.narration: Warm the springs. The gold peak slides earlier. The green bar slides earlier too, but by less. A red bracket can open between them.

scenes.tts: That gap is trophic mismatch. Demand now peaks after the food peak has passed. So an earlier date, on its own, cannot show keeping up.
scenes.visual: Label snaps onto the RED bracket: 'trophic mismatch'. The GREEN bar gets a tag 'earlier' and then a second tag 'still late for its food'.
scenes.narration: That gap is trophic mismatch. Demand now peaks after the food peak has passed. So an earlier date, on its own, cannot show keeping up.

scenes.tts: Does mismatch cost birds? Christiaan Both and colleagues compared nine Dutch populations of the pied flycatcher. It winters in Africa and breeds in European woods.
scenes.visual: Name card 'Both and colleagues, Nature, 2006'. A cartoon pied flycatcher flies a dotted arc from a map of Africa up to the Netherlands, where nine small nest-box pins appear.
scenes.narration: Does mismatch cost birds? Christiaan Both and colleagues compared nine Dutch populations of the pied flycatcher. It winters in Africa and breeds in European woods.

scenes.tts: In some of the forests, caterpillars peaked early. In others they peaked late, and birds that bred early were still well timed.
scenes.visual: Two forests side by side. Left forest 'early food peak': its calendar strip shows the GOLD curve far left of the GREEN bar, with a wide RED bracket. Right forest 'late food peak': GOLD and GREEN still overlap.
scenes.narration: In some of the forests, caterpillars peaked early. In others they peaked late, and birds that bred early were still well timed.

scenes.tts: Where food peaked early, flycatcher numbers fell by about ninety percent over two decades. Where it peaked late, declines were weak at most.
scenes.visual: Under each forest a nest-box count bar starts at a common height labelled 'start'. Over a 'two decades' counter, the left bar shrinks to about one tenth (on-screen: 'about 90% decline'); the right bar shrinks only slightly (on-screen: 'weak decline at most').
scenes.narration: Where food peaked early, flycatcher numbers fell by about ninety percent over two decades. Where it peaked late, declines were weak at most.

scenes.tts: The early forests lost about nine pairs in every ten. Does that comparison prove that mismatch caused the loss?
scenes.visual: The shrunken left bar pulses. Two option tags: 'yes, proven' and 'not yet'.
scenes.narration: The early forests lost about nine pairs in every ten. Does that comparison prove that mismatch caused the loss?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame; a 5-second countdown; caption 'Predict: proof, or not yet?'.

scenes.tts: Not yet. It supports a cost of mismatch, but it compares sites. The forests were not assigned their caterpillar timing, so something else could differ between them.
scenes.visual: The 'not yet' tag lights. A label stamps across both forests: 'comparison, not manipulation'. Small grey question-mark icons (soil, predators, habitat) drift between the two forests.
scenes.narration: Not yet. It supports a cost of mismatch, but it compares sites. The forests were not assigned their caterpillar timing, so something else could differ between them.

scenes.tts: A second question. What tells a bird when to lay? In the field, warm springs bring early laying, but they also bring early food. The pattern alone cannot separate them.
scenes.visual: A field scene: a thermometer and a caterpillar icon both glow beside a great tit cartoon on a nest, with tangled arrows from both to an egg labelled 'earlier laying?'.
scenes.narration: A second question. What tells a bird when to lay? In the field, warm springs bring early laying, but they also bring early food. The pattern alone cannot separate them.

scenes.tts: Marcel Visser and colleagues kept breeding pairs of great tits in climatized aviaries. Every aviary had food freely available. Only the temperature pattern differed, warm or cold.
scenes.visual: Name card 'Visser, Holleman and Caro, 2009'. Two identical mesh aviaries, each with one pair of great tits and a full food dish. The left has a high thermometer and ORANGE tint, the right a low thermometer and cool tint.
scenes.narration: Marcel Visser and colleagues kept breeding pairs of great tits in climatized aviaries. Every aviary had food freely available. Only the temperature pattern differed, warm or cold.

scenes.tts: The warm aviaries generally laid earlier. With food unlimited, the authors read temperature as likely acting as a cue, a signal the birds respond to.
scenes.visual: An egg icon appears earlier on the warm aviary's calendar strip than on the cold one's. Label: 'warm: earlier laying, generally'. Tag: 'temperature: likely a cue'.
scenes.narration: The warm aviaries generally laid earlier. With food unlimited, the authors read temperature as likely acting as a cue, a signal the birds respond to.

scenes.tts: Each design answers its own question. A trend suggests a change. Testing it against chance and natural variation is detection. The forest comparison links food timing to decline, but sites can differ in other ways. The aviaries show temperature acting on laying, in great tits.
scenes.visual: Three side-by-side cards, not a ladder, each headed by its own question. Card 1 'trend: did something change? (detection tests it against chance and natural variation)'. Card 2 'comparison across sites: does food timing go with decline? flycatcher forests (can be confounded)'. Card 3 'manipulation: does temperature move laying? great-tit aviaries (cause, in that preparation)'.
scenes.narration: Each design answers its own question. A trend suggests a change. Testing it against chance and natural variation is detection. The forest comparison links food timing to decline, but sites can differ in other ways. The aviaries show temperature acting on laying, in great tits.

scenes.tts: Through all of it, the date alone never answered the question. What counted was the gap between the food and the family.
scenes.visual: Back to the calendar strip: the GREEN bar's 'earlier' tag fades, while the RED bracket between GOLD peak and GREEN bar stays bright.
scenes.narration: Through all of it, the date alone never answered the question. What counted was the gap between the food and the family.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'Keeping up is judged by the gap, not by the date.'
